reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the CNS
clinicalPearls: A rare malignant intraventricular tumour of the choroid plexus, occurring predominantly in infants and young children
Arises within the ventricular system, most often the lateral ventricles in children, and can disseminate through the cerebrospinal fluid
Overproduction of CSF and ventricular obstruction commonly cause hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure
Distinguished from the benign choroid plexus papilloma by high cellularity, mitotic activity, necrosis and brain invasion
Strongly associated with germline TP53 mutation (Li-Fraumeni syndrome), which should prompt genetic evaluation
The vascular, intraventricular tumour can bleed briskly at surgery, so preoperative planning is important
Treatment centres on maximal safe resection, with chemotherapy and radiotherapy considered according to age and stage
reference.pathophysiology: Choroid plexus carcinoma is a malignant epithelial tumour derived from the choroid plexus epithelium lining the ventricles, the structures responsible for cerebrospinal fluid production. Unlike the well-differentiated papilloma, the carcinoma shows loss of the orderly papillary architecture, marked nuclear atypia, brisk mitotic activity, necrosis and invasion of surrounding brain. Its intraventricular, CSF-bathed location favours dissemination along cerebrospinal fluid pathways. A strong association exists with dysfunction of the TP53 tumour-suppressor pathway, and many tumours arise in children with germline TP53 mutation as part of Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Choroid plexus papilloma and atypical choroid plexus papilloma
Metastatic carcinoma involving the choroid plexus
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced brain MRI to characterise the intraventricular mass and hydrocephalus
Craniospinal MRI to assess for CSF dissemination
CSF cytology for staging once safe
Histopathology, including INI1 staining to exclude rhabdoid tumour
Immunohistochemistry and molecular studies to confirm choroid plexus origin
Germline TP53 testing and assessment for Li-Fraumeni syndrome
redFlags: Rapidly progressive hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure in an infant
Significant intratumoural or perioperative haemorrhage from the vascular mass
Radiological or cytological evidence of CSF dissemination
Germline TP53 mutation with implications for the child and family
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is considerably worse than for choroid plexus papilloma and depends on completeness of resection, metastatic stage and age. Gross total resection improves outcome, but the young age of many patients limits the use of radiotherapy and disease can recur or disseminate; associated Li-Fraumeni syndrome carries additional lifelong cancer risk.
pitfalls: Confusing carcinoma with the benign papilloma and undertreating an aggressive tumour
Underestimating intraoperative bleeding risk from the highly vascular mass
Not testing for germline TP53 and missing Li-Fraumeni syndrome in the child and relatives
Failing to stage the neuraxis and thereby overlooking CSF spread
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
